cells.tense: You feel the imbalance in a close exchange before you sort out whose turn it was.
cells.ask: Tell the person who just gave you something what it gave you. Say the one sentence, then stop talking.
cells.core:
When one side of a close exchange tips, you feel the tip before you can say whose turn it was. People around you get what they're owed from you without you drawing anything up first. There's no arithmetic in it. Something in a day is out of proportion and you already have your hand on it.

That sense is doing work in your friendships and at your table. What it hasn't been given is somewhere to put down what's finished. A relationship that has run its course can be ended without it becoming a sentence about anyone. Letting a thing close is not the same as punishing someone, and it usually clears room for the next thing to start. Fairness here includes the ending.

cells.verb: recognizing what's fair and giving each person their due
cells.place: beside the people you chose, close enough to feel what they carry

cells.tense: You're already carrying the next debt before anyone has asked you for anything.
cells.ask: Choose one balance you've been holding up and leave it alone today. Let the other person close it however they close it.
cells.core:
You're keeping a running tab on the people close to you. Who gave last time, who hasn't matched it, what the next move should be. The counting happens while you're driving and putting dishes away, and it arrives in your tone before you've raised the subject.

Fairness matters and you're not wrong that things tip. The tally has just gotten loud enough that the person across the table hears the ledger instead of you, and hearing it changes what they can say back. When something needs to hold, the trick isn't tracking it harder. It's holding it without squeezing. Let the numbers go quiet for a day and see whether the thing still stands up.

cells.tense: A door closed behind you on the asking, and you still stand at it with your hand down.
cells.ask: Once this week, say what you want back from someone in one plain sentence, then say nothing else.
cells.core:
Claiming what's owed to you is where it stops. You can say what another person should get in a second flat. When the thing is yours, the ask isn't there. A split stays uneven because you let it, and you've gotten used to letting it.

Seeing the imbalance was not the problem. It's the request that went quiet, and requests come back by repetition, not by working up a feeling. Small practice on your own, the kind no one watches, is where the sentence gets steady enough to carry your own weight out loud. Come at it from the solo side first, and let the asking catch up.

cells.tense: You keep the tally running under the table while telling yourself you keep no tally.
cells.ask: Name one thing you're carrying against one person, to yourself, and call it your bother, not theirs.
cells.core:
Certain names make you braced before anything happens. Certain slights get replayed at night, and if asked, you'd say you're the one who lets things go. The weighing runs anyway. The story about it is that there's no story.

What makes it hard to catch is that the reckoning feels like it arrives from nowhere. It doesn't. Somewhere in you, a call was made that something didn't balance, and the call came before you could say why. That's a real read on a room. The mistake is treating the reasons as the point, when the notice was the useful part. When you feel the tally start, trust the notice and look for the argument after.

The act survives being wrong: stopping to name one imbalance out loud still teaches a person where their own fairness-recognition is even if nothing of it is wrong.
